title: Stamenic gets love back after traumatic year
description: Marko Stamenic says "the people around Swansea City" have helped him rediscover his love for football during his first year at the Championship club.
fullText:
Marko Stamenic says "the people around Swansea City" have helped him rediscover his love for football during his first year at the Championship club.

Thursday marked 12 months since Stamenic said farewell to Nottingham Forest to take on the challenge of proving himself in the Championship at Swansea.

The 24-year-old has achieved that feat despite the trauma brought by the sudden death of his father Nikola, who he calls the "main figure" in his development as a player, last October.

As he prepares for Saturday's first home league game of the new season, against Sheffield United, Stamenic reflects on "a year of a lot of ups and downs".

"Probably more off the field for me on a personal note as everybody knows," he says.

"But I think having the people around me in this club, it really helped me cross that hurdle, to find my love again for the game and really get back to how I know I am as a player and person."

Stamenic has missed the "daily conversations" with his father about football.

Then there was this summer's World Cup. Stamenic had been inspired when, as an eight-year-old, he sat alongside his dad to watch New Zealand's games at the 2010 tournament in South Africa.

Sixteen years later, the midfielder made it to football's grandest stage.

All the family were there to see Stamenic feature in New Zealand's three matches in the USA while his dad was "watching from above".

As has been the case at Swansea, Stamenic says, his New Zealand colleagues helped him through.

"I think both really helped in the transition back to, you could say, reality with my normal day-to-day job," he adds.

"The people around, they just they knew what I needed at the time. If it was space, if it was a conversation, they were always a shoulder to lean on."

Stamenic describes the World Cup experience as "amazing" despite the fact that the All Whites exited at the group stage after a draw with Iran and defeats against Egypt and Belgium.

International duty meant a shortened off-season in which Stamenic got engaged to partner Monica before joining up with Swansea during their July training camp in Austria.

Though there is a long second-tier season ahead, Stamenic insists there are no concerns over a lack of summer rest.

"I was telling my missus while we were on holiday, I'm actually missing football a little bit - she wasn't too happy," he says with a smile.

"The club were great. They gave me three weeks off so I had a lot of time to reflect on the World Cup and then just to rest my body and also my mind."

There were no signs of fatigue as Stamenic impressed during Swansea's league opener at Stoke City last weekend.

Latest Swansea City news, analysis and fan views

Matos excited by options as Stewart eyes debut

Listen to the latest Swansea City interviews, news and discussion on BBC Sounds

Playing in a slightly more advanced role, he was involved – alongside fellow central midfielder Jay Fulton – in the build-up to both goals as Vitor Matos' team came from behind to claim a morale-boosting 2-1 victory.

Stamenic is in somewhat unfamiliar territory at the start of this season, given that he is at the same club he represented in the last campaign.

This is a player who had become used to change. Before joining Swansea, he spent a season at Olympiakos – on loan from Forest – having been at Red Star Belgrade in the previous campaign.

The year before that, Stamenic was at Copenhagen.

"It's nice to have some stability now, being familiar with the club, being able to help new players come in," he says.

"I definitely feel like I'm more familiar and I feel like I'm ready to take the next step in my career in the Championship."

Among the new faces trying to settle at Swansea is Elijah Just, Stamenic's international team-mate who managed three goals at the World Cup.

Stamenic says he played a small part in the attacking midfielder's move from Motherwell, having spoken to Just – as well as Swansea chief executive Tom Gorringe – while the deal was in the pipeline.

"I have brought him along now," Stamenic says with another grin.

"He's a talented, a great player, and obviously a great guy. I'm really happy to have him here and I'm hoping the club is going to see what he brings."

Just made his league debut at Stoke alongside fellow new recruits Stephen Welsh, Joseph Opoku and Moussa Yeo.

With another summer addition, Ross Stewart, available for the first time this weekend, Swansea's squad looks fairly healthy, even if there is still work to do in the transfer market.

And after an 11th-place finish last season, Stamenic says Swansea have loftier ambitions for 2026-27 – though he is quick to take a leaf out of Matos' book by insisting all eyes are on the next game.

"There's no hiding the fact that all of our goals and aspirations are to get promoted - we can't lie about that," Stamenic says.

"But on a day-to-day basis, we're just focusing on training, making sure the standard is high, and then when it comes to Saturday, on doing our job."

title: Antonelli leads Norris in Dutch GP first practice
description: Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli heads McLaren's Lando Norris in practice at the Dutch Grand Prix at Zandvoort.
fullText:
Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli headed McLaren's Lando Norris in first practice at the Dutch Grand Prix.

Championship leader Antonelli was 0.121 seconds clear of Norris - who won the last race in Hungary before Formula 1's summer break - with the Italian's Mercedes team-mate George Russell just 0.004secs further adrift.

Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton, who is 50 points behind 19-year-old Antonelli in the championship, was fourth fastest - 0.190secs off the pace.

Hamilton's team-mate Charles Leclerc and the second McLaren of Oscar Piastri completed the top six.

There was an encouraging performance from the new Honda engine in the Aston Martin, with Fernando Alonso ending the session 12th fastest and 1.562secs down.

That appears at first sight to suggest the new engine is providing the 0.3-0.5secs gain in lap time for which Aston Martin had been hoping.

Closer to retiring than changing teams - why Verstappen stayed at Red Bull

Hadjar to miss Dutch Grand Prix with wrist injury

How to follow Dutch Grand Prix on the BBC

If so, it still leaves Honda some way behind the performance of the best engines - as the company itself admits - but it is a step forward from the first iteration of their power-unit Aston Martin have used until now.

Signs Honda are on the right track are what Alonso has been looking for as he ponders whether to stay in the sport beyond the end of the season.

Audi's Nico Hulkenberg was seventh, the quickest driver not to use the soft tyres, with Alpine's Pierre Gasly, the second Audi of Gabriel Bortoleto and Racing Bulls' Arvid Lindblad completing the top 10.

Red Bull's Max Verstappen could manage only 11th fastest, while his team-mate Liam Lawson, promoted from Racing Bulls after regular driver Isack Hadjar broke his wrist while boxing, was 14th.

A number of teams have chassis upgrades, notably Ferrari, who have brought a new floor to this race weekend hoping they can deliver on the potential they showed in Hungary last time, but which frittered away through strategy and operational errors.

At Alpine, only Gasly has the team's first major upgrade for some time, while McLaren and Aston Martin also have small aerodynamic upgrades - McLaren's around the rear bodywork and wing, and Aston Martin's the front wing.

title: Florida high school QB returns to football after leukemia battle, 20 months after last game
description: A leukemia diagnosis sidelined Carter Quinn for his senior season. After an appeal, he's been granted a fifth year of high school football, which starts Friday night.
fullText:
NAPLES, FL — By the time Friday, Aug. 21, rolls around, Carter Quinn will have spent nearly two years waiting to do something that used to be so ordinary he never thought twice about it.

He'll put on a football uniform. He'll walk onto a field. He'll take the first snap of the game at quarterback for St. John Neumann (FL).

And then he'll wait for the whistle.

Quinn knows what happens after that. The other team won't care that he spent months in a hospital. It won't care that chemotherapy took more than 50 pounds from his body or that there was a time when he wasn't sure he'd ever play football again. It won't care about the fifth-year waiver that had to be approved for him to get here.

"I mean, I think I'll definitely take it in for a second, but once the ref blows the whistle, you've got to lock in," Carter said. "No one's thinking about what you've been through or what's going on. Everybody on the other team is just trying to do what they can to win, so no one's thinking about how you feel or what you went through."

For Quinn, that whistle has been a long time coming.

The last time he heard it in a meaningful game, he was still a junior at Lely and a quarterback whose biggest concern was what might come next. He had just thrown for 304 yards and four touchdowns and run for another 71 yards and a score in a 90-56 win over Barron Collier. College football was beginning to enter the conversation. His future, at least as he understood it then, seemed to be opening up in front of him.

Quinn played through it. He finished Lely's season, even though his father, Steve Quinn, knew something wasn't right. After the Trojans lost to Miami Northwestern in the playoffs on Nov. 22, Carter went to have the knee examined.

The ACL tear they found wasn't the biggest problem. The bloodwork was.

His blood-cell count was high. The doctor told the family there were several possibilities, one of which was leukemia. The doctor estimated the odds at 1-to-2%. The family didn't think much of it. There was no history of leukemia in the family, and the possibility seemed remote enough that they went about their lives.

Three weeks later, on Dec. 17, Steve and Carter's mother Lori Quinn were at the Paradise Coast Sports Complex when the doctor called. They were in a staff meeting, and Lori stepped outside to take the call. Steve didn't know what she had heard yet, but he knew something was wrong when he watched his wife fall to the ground.

"I just remember her falling to the ground, and I knew something was wrong," Steve said.

The 1-to-2% possibility they had tried not to think about was no longer a possibility. Carter had leukemia.

That night, Steve and Lori had to tell their son. The next morning, he would begin chemotherapy.

Carter didn't really understand what leukemia meant. His experience with cancer was mostly what he had seen in movies, so the diagnosis hadn't yet taken on the meaning it would later carry. His mind went instead to the thing that had occupied so much of his life.

"'Can I play spring football?' That's the first thing I asked (the doctor)," Carter recalls. "He just kind of looked at me funny. I didn't really know what it was."

He would learn quickly enough. The next 18 months brought spinal taps, lumbar punctures, intravenous chemotherapy and medications designed to fight the abnormal blood cells. Hospital stays became part of the routine, with one standing rule: If Carter's temperature reached 101 degrees, he had to go back.

Steve remembers one such night particularly well. Carter had been home for only two hours after spending four or five days in the hospital when his temperature reached 101. They had to take him back. Remarkably, Steve said, that was the only time during the entire process he remembers his son complaining.

"He just did the deal," Steve said. "He never, ever complained. The only time — one time — he complained was when he just got home from the hospital. He was there for four or five days, and anytime he got to a 101-degree temperature, he had to go to the hospital. He literally got home, and within two hours he got a 101-degree temperature, and we had to take him back.

"That's the only time I ever heard him complain during these 18 months. He was just a trooper."

The physical changes were harder for Carter to ignore. He had been playing at roughly 190 pounds at Lely. During treatment, he eventually fell to about 138. A few months into it, he began to realize just how much his body had changed.

"A little bit later, a couple months into treatment, I kind of realized, 'Dang, my body's changing,'" Carter said. "There were definitely thoughts of, 'I don't think I'll ever play the game again.' Once the idea of the extra year came, it kind of was there, but there was definitely a big period where I didn't think I'd ever play football again."

For a while, there wasn't much Carter could do about those thoughts. His body needed to recover, and football had to wait. But stepping away from the game entirely was never really an option for him.

When Lely's 2025 season arrived, Carter couldn't play. His younger brother Brady, who transferred from First Baptist, could, and Carter wanted to be around him and the program. So he kept showing up at practices, usually in a Lely jacket and sweats, and looked for ways to contribute. Former Lely coach Ben Hammer gave him a headset, and Carter began helping where he could — offering encouragement, pointing out small things and occasionally coaching Brady, who was two years younger.

It wasn't a formal coaching assignment. Carter wanted to help, Hammer said, and the headset gave him a way to remain involved with the team he had spent the previous season leading on the field.

There were days when even that was difficult. The effects of chemotherapy sometimes made it hard for Carter to put on tennis shoes, so Hammer made an exception to one of his standing practice rules. Nobody was supposed to show up in slides or flip-flops. Carter still wanted to be at practice, though, and Hammer wasn't going to let a rule keep him away.

"He still wanted to be at practice, to be around his brothers," Hammer said. "And when I say his brother, not just his actual brother, but mentor Luke Trebilcock, our JV quarterback, and help with that young but talented wide receiver crew we had."

For Carter, being around the team offered something that treatment couldn't. He couldn't take a snap, but he could still talk football. He could watch Brady. He could help younger players. He could remain connected to the routine and the people that had been such a large part of his life before his diagnosis.

Hammer came to see that as part of Carter's recovery, too.

"And I think that he would tell you that that was part of his healing process," Hammer said. "And, for lack of a better term, like, the winning process against leukemia was being at Lely football every day and how much his friends and buddies did to kind of encourage him and keep him going in the right direction."

Carter's presence also became a reminder of what the Lely program had been missing. He was still the quarterback everyone knew, only now he was watching from the sideline instead of taking the snaps. His friends didn't let him disappear completely. Lely began putting orange, football-shaped stickers on their helmets with CQ8 printed in black — a small tribute to Carter's initials and the No. 8 he had always worn. That ultimately spread to neighboring high schools.

Brady wore the number himself during the 2025 season for his brother.

His decision to remain at Lely carried its own significance. Brady had opportunities to attend a national-level football program, Hammer said, but chose to stay with his brother and family during a difficult period. Carter couldn't play, but his brother was still wearing his number and playing the game they had grown up around together.

For Carter, that season offered an unusual version of football. He wasn't competing. He wasn't preparing for college recruiting. He was simply trying to get healthy enough to have another chance.

For much of that winter, there was no clear indication of when — or whether — Carter would look like that player again. His focus was on getting through treatment. Football remained important, but for the first time in his life, it was something he could only watch from the outside.

For a long time, getting back to football was something Carter could only imagine. Then, in the spring, the possibility began to feel more tangible.

On March 2, 2026 Carter had his port removed. He was still undergoing treatment, but doctors told him that if his platelets and hemoglobin were where they needed to be, he could begin working out and lifting again, eventually progressing to contact football. After spending so long watching his body become weaker, Carter finally had something concrete to work toward.

"As soon as they told him that he was free and cleared to play, you just could tell the look in his eye was all different," Steve Quinn said. "He just was motivated."

Football wasn't the only thing that helped him get through the months when he couldn't play. Through Make-A-Wish, Carter received a boat, giving him a way to spend time on the water with his family and another activity that didn't require him to push his recovering body the way football would. Fishing became something he could look forward to, while the possibility of returning to the field remained somewhere in the distance.

"I would say just being on the water is really peaceful," Carter said. "It's kind of something you can do when it's not getting tackled by the linemen and stuff. Something that also kept my mind off of it was the fact that I would have the chance to play football again if it did come through, and just to keep pushing through because the end goal was to play football again and keep going after all my dreams. It was the fact that I had that in the back of my mind, that I could do it again."

"The first couple months, we really had to take it slow and just get my body back," Carter said. "But once it started kicking, we were just full go. He's been with me for the nutrition part, just spiritually, mentally, and he's just been there step by step. He puts his focus on me and just walks me through it. He's the person who really got my body back to what it was."

The progress became measurable. Carter began eating three meals a day, something that hadn't always been possible during treatment, and started putting weight back on. He threw regularly with Ken Mastrole, a quarterbacks coach in Southwest Florida, and continued lifting as his body allowed. By August, he was up to 179 pounds, just 11 pounds shy of where he had been when he was playing for Lely.

"When I started working out again, I started at like 145 pounds, I think, and now I'm up to 179 as of yesterday," Carter said. "Just putting muscle on, putting weight on and eating healthy, treating my body like a temple and all that. Like I said, not taking nothing for granted."

Carter still wants to get back to 190. But he's not necessarily chasing the exact version of himself who played at Lely. He believes the body he's rebuilding may ultimately be different from the one he had before leukemia.

"I think I was a lot thicker playing at Lely, but I think I have a lot more cut muscle," Carter said. "If I'm at 185 to 187, I'll be okay with that."

That process became another part of the comeback. Lely principal Jennifer Bledsoe and Hammer worked with legendary Naples head coach Bill Kramer, who went up to Gainesville in person to lobby on Quinn's behalf, while Carter's family gathered what was needed to make its case. After spending so much of the previous year having little control over what his body could do, Carter was now waiting on a group of people he'd never met to decide whether he could play the game he had spent his life preparing for.

The hearing was held April 8. Carter, Steve, Lori and Sean Phillips, a close friend who had a hand in getting him the boat, gathered for a Zoom meeting with a sectional committee within the FHSAA. They answered questions and explained Carter's circumstances, then waited while the committee considered the request.

The meeting lasted about 15 minutes.

Then a motion was made to approve Carter's fifth year. There was a very quick second.

After 18 months of wondering whether football was gone from his life for good, Carter had his answer.

"I was really happy," Carter said. "I kind of had the feeling I knew I was going to get it because Miss Bledsoe and Coach Hammer worked really hard and worked with Coach Kramer, who used to be on that board. They worked really hard to help me get it, but it was just a relief because I knew I would get my life back on track."

That last part is what mattered most to Carter. The fifth year wasn't simply another season on a football schedule. It gave him back a routine he had lost when leukemia took him away from the field. Shortly after the ruling was made, he made an announcement that he'd be transferring to St. John Neumann.

"Football, it's always been football, so that's all I know," Carter said. "It was kind of getting back into that routine of working out and then playing, so I was just really happy."

Steve had watched the entire process from a different perspective. He had watched people rally around his son when Carter couldn't play, then watched Carter rebuild his body when doctors finally allowed him to return to physical activity. Now, after all the uncertainty, the answer was no longer dependent on what might happen. Carter had been given another season.

Steve remembers his son's reaction being much simpler than the months of work that had gone into getting there.

For Carter, the approval didn't erase what had happened. He was still undergoing treatment, and his doctors would not consider him officially in remission until a later point in the process. It didn't put the weight back on his frame overnight or turn him immediately into the quarterback he'd been at Lely.

What it did was give him something he had spent months without: a date to work toward.

And this time, there was a football field at the end of it.

In July, Carter finally got to do something he had spent more than a year imagining: He walked onto a football practice field wearing a helmet again.

Not a headset. Not a Lely jacket and sweats. A helmet.

And at St. John Neumann, there was no competition for the quarterback job. It was Carter's.

The routine he had once taken for granted had become the thing he had worked toward for months. Conditioning. Lifting. Throwing. Walking into a locker room with teammates. Getting pushed hard by a coach. All of it had taken on a different meaning after spending so much time away from it.

"You're not taking anything for granted," Carter said. "You used to be like, 'Oh, we're conditioning,' and now you're like, 'Damn, it is awesome that you get to be out here.' You never think about how much you would just like being around the guys in the locker room when you're not. You don't think about the little things, and now you just appreciate everything. When something's taken away from you, it just makes you realize so much."

The quarterback wearing No. 8 is also different from the one who wore it at Lely. After the tributes with helmet stickers and his brother wearing the number, it's now back on Carter, who has spent the entire summer preparing to start again.

The football return, however, has come before the medical journey is officially finished. Carter said he currently has no cancer cells in his body, but his doctors won't technically consider him in remission until he reaches the required point in his treatment. For now, he is taking pills and continuing to follow the treatment plan that began after his diagnosis in December 2024.

That reality has changed Carter's perspective on what it means to return. Before leukemia, football was simply what he did. Now, after having it taken away, he understands how much of his life was wrapped up in things he barely noticed.

Steve has noticed the change, too. The son who went through treatment is not the same teenager who entered his junior season at Lely, and the difference has little to do with how much weight Carter has regained or how well he throws a football.

"He has become a different kid," Steve said. "I can't imagine what has gone through his head over the last 18 months, but his maturity level and his awareness and just who he is as a person has totally changed."

That may be the biggest difference between the quarterback who left the field against Barron Collier and the one who will return Friday night.

The first time Carter played after his diagnosis won't be about proving that he beat leukemia. He hasn't reached that point yet. It won't be about proving that he can be the same quarterback he was before, either. His body is different, his perspective is different and his life has changed in ways that can't be measured by passing yards or touchdowns.

It will simply be another football game.

St. John Neumann will host Monsignor Pace of Miami at 7:30 p.m. Friday. Carter will take the first snap at quarterback, something that once would have been so routine that he never would have thought twice about it.

He knows what it is like to stand on the outside and watch somebody else play. He knows what it is like to wonder if he'll ever get the chance again.

And he knows that once the whistle blows, none of that matters to the other team.

"It's like everybody's playing for themselves, really," Carter Quinn said. "There's no sympathy for me on the field, so that's why I've got to get back to that point where I can be that guy that I was and go just tear it up."

For nearly two years, Carter has been waiting for that whistle.

Friday night, he'll finally hear it again.

title: Michigan State football 2026 game-by-game predictions: UCLA
description: Predicting every Michigan State football game for the 2026 season -- next up is a road conference game against the UCLA Bruins
fullText:
Michigan State football is right around the corner so it's time to start predicting how the season will shake out for the Spartans.

Michigan State football is under new leadership this season, with Pat Fitzgerald set to take over as the next head coach. He will take over a program looking to get back on the winning side, with the Spartans in the midst of a four-year bowl drought. Can he get the job done and get the Spartans back to a bowl game this season? I have offered my thoughts on that in our game-by-game predictions segment on Spartans Wire.

We continue on with the next of my game-by-game predictions for each of the matchups on the Spartans' 2026 schedule. Each morning a new prediction will be released following Michigan State's schedule. Next up is a Big Ten matchup against UCLA…

Location: Rose Bowl Stadium (Pasadena, Calif.)

This will only mark the eighth meeting all-time between Michigan State and UCLA, with the Bruins winning the last four games after the Spartans won the first three. Michigan State last beat UCLA in 1965.

The most recent meeting came last year when UCLA throttled the Spartans during Homecoming weekend for an upset victory. That early October loss sparked the narrative of Michigan State needing to move on from former head coach Jonathan Smith, which eventually was the case after the season concluded.

MSU predicted record: 5-2 (3-1 in Big Ten)

Michigan State is riding high coming into this game, with the Spartans ranked for the first time since 2022 following back-to-back home wins against Illinois and Northwestern to move to 5-2 overall and 3-1 in Big Ten play. The Spartans can clinch bowl eligibility for the first time since 2021 with a win over the Bruins in LA.

UCLA has became the darling bounce-back team for many across the country this offseason, but I personally envision them struggling out of the gate. I have the Bruins sitting at 2-4 overall (2-2 in Big Ten) with a notable win over the Wisconsin Badgers in the week prior to Michigan State visiting.

Michigan State has struggled when they head out west and I believe that trend continues in this road matchup against the Bruins. On paper, this should be a toss-up but a few critical turnovers by the Spartans tilt this one in favor of the Bruins and kills any wild dreams of Michigan State contending for a Big Ten championship.

The Spartans will be on a bye next week before heading into their annual rivalry game with the Michigan Wolverines…

Next on the game-by-game predictions list is a road Big Ten game vs. Michigan. That prediction will be released tomorrow.

title: 5 keys to victory for the Rams against the Saints
description: These are the five things the Rams must do to beat the Saints in their preseason game on Saturday.
fullText:
The Los Angeles Rams are set to take on the New Orleans Saints in preseason action on Saturday, and for the players suiting up, this game could be the difference between a spot on the 53-man roster and being waived. With so much on the line, here are five keys to victory, both for the Rams and individual players.

While we need to see more from Stetson Bennett and Ty Simpson, the constant movement of the pocket last week served as a good foundation to evaluate both players. The offensive line played well, but there's no reason to risk a sitting duck.

If the Rams want to push the ball downfield, these quarterbacks will need room to plant and throw. Ensuring the quarterback won't be a stationary target will be critical to accomplishing that goal.

Hunter's roster spot is in question, and we have yet to see what the thumping ball carrier can do when he gets a head full of steam. Screens, swings, something. He's getting caught at the line of scrimmage, and it's preventing fans and media from seeing what he can really do in space.

Bailey's length was noted last week, and he's been making strides in practice. If he continues to improve, Bailey could become a pass-rushing specialist. While his length gives him an advantage on the outside, I'd like to see Bailey lined up and utilized in a variety of ways, just to see exactly where he's at and to understand what the scope of his abilities is.

Max Klare and Mark Redman were fantastic against Kansas City, and they should be the difference against New Orleans due to their height and pass-catching skills. If they continue to develop, not only would the Rams have five starting-caliber tight ends on the roster, but Redman could be a perfect option to activate off the practice squad if needed.

When Tyler Higbee got hurt last season, the Rams shelved their 13-personnel offense. Their development means the Rams won't have to do that in 2026.

Evans didn't have the best game last week, which was the opposite of kicker Harrison Mevis. The special teams look improved as a whole, with Evans being the only question mark. Just make sure he's fine with some solid punts, as the last thing this team needs is to overlook a looming issue.

title: Nick Bolton on the impact of two veteran players during training camp
description: During his press conference, Kansas City Chiefs linebacker Nick Bolton discussed the impact of Patrick Mahomes and Travis Kelce at camp | @EdEastonJr
fullText:
Kansas City Chiefs linebacker Nick Bolton spoke with reporters after practice on Thursday at Missouri Western State University. He shared what he believes was the best part of watching Patrick Mahomes rehab over the last nine months.

"Just seeing how much he's (Patrick Mahomes) committed to the team. It doesn't have to be that way; he came in as the season was over with. I came back just to pack up my stuff, and he was already there. I came back a couple of times throughout the summer, and he was there," said Bolton. "I think I came down, took a vacation for a week, and he came back and was there, so his commitment to the team and how much it means to him on a personal level, but also for just being a first teammate for his brothers."

Bolton opened up about the impact of having Travis Kelce out here each camp with him, without missing practices, even though he's the oldest player on the team.

"Yeah, obviously he's (Travis Kelce) getting a bit older in the years, but the resiliency- showing up every day even if he doesn't feel 100 percent- he gives as much as he can, 100 percent of what he has," said Bolton, "That resonates with the team. There's no excuses when you have the old guy out there running routes and stuff like that. It's been fun to watch him work."

The future of Mahomes with the Chiefs was solidified during the offseason with his massive contract extension while he awaits his official return to the field. Kelce could have possibly appeared in his last training camp.

title: Former Washington QB gets next NFL shot with New York Giants
description: Former Washington Huskies quarterback Jake Haener signed with the New York Giants on Monday, where he will compete for a backup job.
fullText:
Jake Haener has earned another shot at an NFL roster.

The former Washington quarterback, who was taken in the fourth round of the 2023 NFL draft by the New Orleans Saints after transferring from Montlake to Fresno State, signed with the New York Giants on Monday morning. It's Haener's third team in 2026 after finishing the 2025 regular season on the Saints practice squad, then signing a reserve/futures contract with the Kansas City Chiefs before being waived in May.

The #Giants are signing veteran QB Jake Haener, source says. Haener, who had worked out for the team late last month, lands in East Rutherford after a few workouts with other teams. pic.twitter.com/s0TjX8Iojo

Haener appeared in only 4 games at Washington, all in 2018, completing 9 of his 13 passes for 107 yards with 1 touchdown and 1 interception. He nearly returned to the Huskies in 2022; however, after Washington hired Fresno State coach Kalen DeBoer to replace Jimmy Lake. DeBoer wanted Haener to follow him back to Montlake, but a credits issue and the subsequent re-hire of Jeff Tedford at Fresno State kept Haener with the Bulldogs. DeBoer pivoted to Indiana quarterback Michael Penix Jr., whom he had coached as the Hoosiers' offensive coordinator in 2019.

That decision, of course, worked out for Washington. Penix went on to become a Heisman finalist and led the Huskies to a national championship game appearance in 2023 before being selected No. 8 overall by the Atlanta Falcons in the 2024 NFL draft.

Haener has played in 8 NFL games, starting 1, all for the Saints in 2024. He has completed 18 of 39 career passing attempts for 226 yards with a touchdown and an interception. But after Giants third-string quarterback Brandon Allen struggled in the team's first preseason game, Haener has a real opportunity to win that job and join second-year passer Jaxson Dart and veteran backup Jameis Winston in New York's quarterback room.

After transferring to Fresno State, Haener set the program record for career completion percentage at 68.1 percent, finished in the top five of every major passing statistic, earned All-Mountain West honors twice, was named a captain all three years, and was named MVP of the 2023 Senior Bowl. He is one of three Bulldogs to throw for at least 4,000 yards in a season, along with brothers David and Derek Carr.

The Giants travel to Florida to play the Miami Dolphins on Saturday for their second of three preseason games. New York ends their preseason with a crosstown game against the New York Jets on August 28, two days before the 53-man roster deadline.

title: Like his brother, Gino van Steenis sees PFL gold in his future
description: Gino van Steenis believes he's growing every day as a fighter, and has his sights set on a championship in the near future.
fullText:
Gino Van Steenis aims to prove his steady growth at PFL Tampa.

Van Steenis (8-2) competes on the prelims against Robert Watley in a lightweight bout at Benchmark International Arena in Tampa, Fla. It's a chance to stretch his current winning streak to three, and even though he's put together back-to-back stoppages, he hopes to do more to impress the fans.

"I'm just starting," van Steenis told MMA Junkie Radio. "I really feel like every fight I'm getting better. Every training I'm getting better. I didn't show yet, the people, what I'm capable of, and I really want to show it every fight. I think it's now my time."

The van Steenis name carries a lot of weight in the PFL promotion, as Gino's older and bigger brother, Costello, is the former middleweight champion. He hopes to follow in those footsteps in the near future, but knows there is more work to be done first.

"I think I'm not so far," Gino said. "I'm not there yet; I know I'm not there yet. I'm growing better every week, every month, and I'm training with the best people – and I'm there. They're not better than me. I think I need a little bit more experience, and I can be a champion within – I don't know, one day. Give me the chance – but I think in two years, I'm definitely a champion."

Watley (16-4) is 1-1 under the PFL banner, and comes into this fight after a 34-second knockout loss against Dakota Bush in March, which snapped a five-fight winning streak. Gino sees the opportunity to put another stoppage loss on his opponent's record, but isn't quite sure which round it may come.

"In my head, it's gonna be a finish," Gino said. "I really don't know if it's gonna be in the first round. It can be. I don't know if it's gonna be in the second round or the third round, but I really believe with all my heart, it's gonna be a finish. It's gonna be a knockout."

This article originally appeared on MMA Junkie: Like his brother, Gino van Steenis sees PFL gold in his future

title: Report: Lakers ownership saga likely won't impact Luka Doncic's future
description: If Luka Doncic does leave the Lakers within the next couple of years, it likely won't be because of their ownership saga, according to one report.
fullText:
The Los Angeles Lakers' ownership situation may be in flux right now, but it hasn't changed their outlook on the court. They have assembled what should be a competitive, if not an elite, roster for the upcoming NBA season, and in Luka Doncic, they have one of the best basketball players in the world who just entered the prime of his career.

One cloud hanging over the franchise's not-too-distant future is Doncic's ability to opt out of his contract and become a free agent in 2028. While no one right now expects the Slovenian to leave the team, it remains within the realm of possibilities if he feels the organization isn't making enough strides toward winning the championship.

According to one report, if Doncic does depart, it may not be because of the Lakers' ownership saga. That is what Sean Deveney wrote in a recent article for Heavy Sports.

"Talking to people around the NBA, the feeling is that all this is not likely to have much impact on what happens with Doncic going forward. He will be eligible to sign an extension next summer, and until his signature is on the contract, there will be angst in the organization."

Deveney then noted that Doncic "does not want to move around much" and "would prefer to be a legacy guy with one franchise," which would point to him remaining with the Purple and Gold for some time.

The two-time scoring champ was traded to L.A. in February 2025 by the Dallas Mavericks in a shocking trade that rocked the NBA like a magnitude 9.9 earthquake. He was just eight months removed from carrying the Mavs to the NBA Finals after finishing with the fifth seed in the Western Conference, and while it took him some time to emotionally process the trade, he eventually seemed to accept that L.A. is the place to be for him.

He has the opportunity to lead the storied franchise to at least one championship in the coming years, provided he keeps taking better care of his body and the franchise takes care of fully building a championship-caliber cast around him. That kind of opportunity would be extremely hard for a player of his caliber to walk away from.

Doncic is currently holding a minicamp for his Lakers teammates in his native Slovenia. That isn't exactly the type of behavior that would suggest he's planning some sort of exit strategy.

title: Class of 2022 Ole Miss DL enters transfer portal after gaining eligibility
description: Former Ole Miss Rebels defensive tackle Zxavian Harris became one of many from the class of 2022 to gain eligibilty and enter the transfer portal.
fullText:
New Orleans Saints defensive lineman Zxavian Harris became one of many players from the NCAA's class of 2022 to regain eligibility. He has entered the transfer portal after earning a temporary restraining order from the NCAA, according to Matt Zenitz.

Harris, along with several NFL players from the class of 2022, has gained eligibility thanks to a ruling that anyone from the class of 2022 who didn't redshirt, get drafted, or sign an NFL contract earns one more season. That list includes his Ole Miss teammate DaeQuan Wright. The court ruling on Aug. 19 made their return to college football possible.

Harris played his entire four-season career with the Ole Miss Rebels. The defensive lineman racked up 123 combined tackles, 17.5 tackles for loss, 5.5 sacks, one interception, three pass breakups, and one forced fumble.

He went undrafted in the 2026 NFL Draft, but the Saints signed him as a UDFA. However, they cut him on Aug. 8, 2026, opening the door for him to play college football again.

However, a reunion was quashed pretty quickly. On Aug. 6, Ole Miss coach Pete Golding said he was not inclined to add any new players to the roster unless outside circumstances, like an injury, change the situation. He said he does not want to displace someone currently on the roster.

The SEC has reinforced that no player is allowed to transfer from one SEC school to another, so that leaves the Big Ten and ACC open for his services. Regardless, Harris would be a big addition for any college team looking to compete for a championship.

title: Antonelli holds off nearest rivals to top practice session at Dutch GP
description: Kimi Antonelli topped the sole practice session at the Dutch Grand Prix but British trio Lando Norris, Lewis Hamilton and George Russell look well set to challenge the championship leader. The Italian, who turns 20 next week, has returned from the sport's summer shutdown with a 50-point lead over Hamilton at the top of the standings, with his Mercedes team-mate Russell nine further back.
fullText:
Kimi Antonelli topped the sole practice session at the Dutch Grand Prix but British trio Lando Norris, Lewis Hamilton and George Russell look well set to challenge the championship leader.

The Italian, who turns 20 next week, has returned from the sport's summer shutdown with a 50-point lead over Hamilton at the top of the standings, with his Mercedes team-mate Russell nine further back.

Antonelli has won six races in the grid's dominant car but Hamilton and Russell hope to begin reeling him in - starting this weekend in the seaside town of Zandvoort.

Hamilton believes he has returned in great shape from the break and led the way as practice came towards a conclusion.

But first Norris and then Antonelli found the answer, the Italian finishing the session 0.121 seconds clear of the reigning world champion.

Russell pipped Hamilton to third, with Ferrari's Charles Leclerc fifth - less than three tenths separating the top five cars to hint at a tight battle for sprint pole later on Friday.

Ferrari and McLaren have brought significant upgrades this weekend as they seek to claw back the gap to Antonelli and Mercedes.

Hamilton's consistency has kept him in the championship hunt. He is the only driver to have completed every race lap so far this season, with his one win coming in Barcelona in June.

Norris is refusing to give up hope of defending his title after claiming a first win of the season last time out in Budapest, despite being 91 points off the pace.

Max Verstappen, whose new long-term Red Bull deal was announced on Thursday, finished the session down in 11th.

title: Joshua fight doesn't look like it will happen - Fury
description: Tyson Fury says his fight with Anthony Joshua "doesn't look like it's going to happen" in a verbal tirade against his British rival and promoter Eddie Hearn posted on social media.
fullText:
Tyson Fury says his fight with Anthony Joshua "doesn't look like it's going to happen" in a verbal tirade against his British rival and promoter Eddie Hearn posted on social media.

The pair had been expected to meet in November in one of the biggest fights in British boxing history, but uncertainty over where the bout will take place has cast fresh doubt over the deal.

Joshua and his promoter Hearn have signed a contract for it to be staged in the United Kingdom, while Saudi organisers are pushing for a move to the United States.

"Doesn't look like they're going to sign the fight and it doesn't look like it's going to happen all because Eddie Hearn and that want more money," Fury said in a series of Instagram stories.

Joshua and Fury have separate contracts with Saudi Arabian-owned Sela. New York's Madison Square Garden is understood to be Sela's preference so that the fight - which will broadcast on Netflix - can cater for American audiences.

On Thursday, Hearn told IFL TV that a list of changes required for the fight to take place in America had been sent to Sela.

Hearn says the main change concerns compensation for Joshua because of the different tax implications of fighting in America.

"In layman's terms, by staging the fight in America, Anthony Joshua receives less money than he would do if the fight was in the UK where he was contractually agreed," he said.

Fury responded by calling Joshua and Hearn "disgusting" and "money-thirsty".

"It is what it is. Same old cliche a decade later. Keep running you little cowards," he added.

In further posts containing expletives, Fury called Hearn a "bag carrier" and criticised Joshua's mindset.

"I'll move on and fight somebody else but just know you never had the guts to fight Tyson Fury, ever, you little coward," Fury added.

After chaotic return, where does Joshua win leave Fury fight?

Joshua signs deal to fight Fury - Hearn

Fury v Joshua could be held overnight at Wembley

In addition to the request for increased compensation, Hearn said his list of addenda covers practical matters including travel, accreditation and media arrangements.

Hearn said it had been approved by Joshua and his lawyer before being sent to Sela.

"We've had no feedback yet," Hearn said, adding that he had not heard from Sela for three or four days.

Reports on Thursday suggested a list of changes had been presented to the Saudi organisers. Hearn claims those reports were based on a leaked email and insists the issues raised in it were not part of the list sent to Sela.

"The addendum does not have one of those points raised in that leaked email," he said.

Hearn did confirm Matchroom held a meeting with Sela regarding money owed to the organisation for previously agreed contracts.

He said those issues, which reportedly included payments relating to darts and snooker events, international promotional fees, the World Series of Darts, the Ronnie O'Sullivan Snooker Academy in Riyadh and money owed to Matchroom from previous boxing events, were separate from the Joshua-Fury contract.

Hearn did not directly address claims that Joshua was still owed money from his most recent fight against Kristian Prenga.

"I'm not going to go into that at the moment. That's a contractual position that will be left for another day," he said.

BBC Sport has contacted Sela for comment.

The situation has been complicated by the arrival of the Dana White-fronted Zuffa Boxing, which is jointly owned by Sela and TKO Group Holdings. TKO is the managing partner, while White is among the promotion's executive leaders.

Hearn has criticised the push to stage the fight in America.

"The reason that this is happening, to be completely honest with you, is because TKO and Zuffa have basically convinced or tried to convince Turki that this fight is massive in America," he said.

Fury also addressed White's involvement.

"White wants to be involved, he can come on my side. He can be a part of me. Get in, Dana. You want to make the fight, you can come on my side," Fury said.

BBC Sport has also contacted TKO for comment.

Joshua and Fury are two of the biggest names in British boxing and have become crossover stars during their careers.

There has been strong support from within British boxing for the fight to take place in the UK.

Hearn said the importance of staging it in Britain had nothing to do with how many fans could attend.

"It's about British boxing. It's about amateur boxing clubs. It's about kids watching the biggest fight in boxing in our country," he said.

He also highlighted Joshua's history in Britain, including winning Olympic gold at London 2012.

"And more than that, it's about Anthony Joshua wanting to have this fight in Britain where he won the Olympic gold medal, where he won the World Championship, where he absolutely changed the face of boxing forever," Hearn added.

title: Here we go: Barcelona reach €4 million agreement for veteran goalkeeper, who will arrve in 2027
description: According to SPORT, Fenerbahçe have accepted FC Barcelona’s offer for Dominik Livakovic, and the operation has now entered its final stage. Barring a surprise, the 31-year-old goalkeeper will becom...
fullText:
According to SPORT, Fenerbahçe have accepted FC Barcelona's offer for Dominik Livakovic, and the operation has now entered its final stage.

Barring a surprise, the 31-year-old goalkeeper will become a new Barça player in 2027.

The club will shortly begin the necessary paperwork to complete a signing worth around €4 million.

Fabrizio Romano has given the customary 'Here we go' to the operation, confirming that the deal is worth €2 million in fixed fee plus another €2 million in add-ons.

Once the deal is finalized, the intention is to loan the goalkeeper out for one season so that he can return next summer and join the Barcelona squad.

Barcelona are planning ahead for the future of their goalkeeping department.

With Wojciech Szczesny entering the final year of his contract, the sporting department wants a reliable successor lined up and believes Livakovic has the qualities needed to join Joan Garcia from next season onward.

There should not be any problems from the player's side either. The Croatian goalkeeper is very keen on the possibility of joining Barça and is now waiting for the final steps of the operation to be completed.

The formula will allow Livakovic to continue playing regularly this season before making his definitive move to Barcelona.

Barça believe that securing the deal for a figure close to €4 million represents a good market opportunity and allows them to address an important position well in advance.

A familiar figure in Barcelona's offices once again features in the operation.

Andy Bara has maintained an excellent relationship with Barça's sporting department for years, particularly with Deco and Joan Laporta. That trust has been built through several operations over recent seasons.

Set to join Barcelona in 2027. (Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images)

The Croatian agent has been involved in important deals for the club, including operations involving Dani Olmo and Joan Garcia.

Barcelona particularly value his willingness to find solutions, even when negotiations become complicated.

Now the two sides have come together again over Livakovic. The strong relationship between Bara and the Blaugrana has once again helped an operation reach a decisive stage.

With Fenerbahce having accepted the offer, the next step will be to complete the paperwork, finalize the goalkeeper's signing and then arrange his loan for the coming season.

title: Santiago Espinal signs minor league deal with Diamondbacks
description: The Dodgers roster has been a carousel of All-Star (both current and former) talent playing nearly every day and the taxi squad members whose role is equally vital to the team’s success. One of those former taxi squad members, Santiago Espinal, has found a new home within the NL West. Espinal signed a minor league […]
fullText:
The Dodgers roster has been a carousel of All-Star (both current and former) talent playing nearly every day and the taxi squad members whose role is equally vital to the team's success.

One of those former taxi squad members, Santiago Espinal, has found a new home within the NL West. Espinal signed a minor league deal with the Arizona Diamondbacks on Thursday, as per an announcement from the Triple-A Reno Aces via X.

It's been a chaotic 2026 season for Espinal, who initially latched onto a minor league deal with the Dodgers and eventually made the opening day roster. He played in 36 games with the big league squad, slashing .268/.276/.375 with a home run and seven RBI across 60 plate appearances. He was released by the Dodgers on June 18 before signing a minor league deal with the Texas Rangers on July 2, only to once again be released 26 days later. Espinal slashed .262/.333/.310 with six RBI with the Triple-A Round Rock Express.

Right now the biggest talking point for the Dodgers outside of Shohei Ohtani's battle for MVP is the turbulent, lackluster first year of the Kyle Tucker experience. As the Dodgers prepare to open a three-game set against the Pittsburgh Pirates on Friday, all eyes will be pointed towards Tucker and whether he'll continue to underperform at home or possibly find his old, pre-Dodger self at the plate.

Mookie Betts and Miguel Rojas both sat down and spoke about Tucker's difficult season in the most recent episode of the On Base with Mookie Betts podcast, where Rojas touched on having his teammate's back despite the challenges.

"I have all my confidence in Tucker… I am a true believer that when you feel good, you play good. When you're going out there everyday knowing the guys have your back, it's a good feeling… I really want him to believe that the opinions that matter are the ones that are to your left and to your right."

Bill Shaikin of the Los Angeles Times reports that Cox customers will finally be able to watch Dodger games on SportsNet LA.

On Friday, for the first time in 13 years, Cox subscribers within the Dodgers' broadcast territory will be able to watch the team on their local television home. Fans can find SportsNet LA on Channel 63 in Orange County, Channel 54 in Palos Verdes, Channel 36 in Santa Barbara and Channel 50 in Las Vegas.

Johnathan Mayo, Jim Callis and Sam Dykstra of MLB.com picked Josue de Paula as the Dodgers prospect most likely to get a big league callup this year.

title: Estre “on an extremely short leash” following Road America collision, says IMSA’s Barfield
description: IMSA Race Director Beaux Barfield issued a stern warning that the Porsche factory driver could be watching from the sidelines if involved in another on-track clash
fullText:
IMSA Race Director Beaux Barfield clarified the sanctioning body's decision to place Porsche Penske Motorsport driver Kévin Estre on probation rather than an immediate suspension following his late-race clash with Jack Aitken at Road America, warning that any further missteps will quickly sideline the Frenchman.

Speaking to media on Thursday ahead of the GT-only weekend at Virginia International Raceway, Barfield addressed questions surrounding the penalty following the destructive incident during the Aug. 2 Motul SportsCar Endurance Grand Prix. Despite both GTP entries ending up in the barriers, Barfield cited a decade of disciplinary history as the driving factor behind issuing a two-race probation instead of a ban.

"If there was any discussion about suspension, that was not in line with precedent that had been established for probation and suspension over the last, let's say, 10 years," Barfield said. "So if there was discussion about that, it ended up, well, the precedent really for an offense like this with the history that we've had with these teams and these drivers was such that it was 

"And that's a long way of saying that it was a deeper discussion to say precedent became really the prevailing point on how the decision, the final decision was probation over suspension."

However, Barfield made it clear that IMSA officials will not tolerate a repeat performance. When pressed on how race control will police Estre during his probationary period, Barfield delivered a direct warning.

"He's on an extremely short leash that could lead to him serving the remainder of his probation on the sideline. That's the intent. That's the purpose of it," Barfield said. "In terms of trying to give you some understanding on how long that leash is, I think that would be pretty difficult. But if he's involved in similar on-track incidents, then I think he'll be finished pretty quickly."

A look back at the final restart from @roadamerica. pic.twitter.com/IDncRtG4nG

The controversy stems from a dramatic restart in the closing minutes of the six-hour endurance round at the 4.048-mile Road America circuit. With just over 10 minutes remaining, Estre in the #6 Porsche 963 and Aitken in the #31 Whelen Cadillac V-Series.R were locked in a fierce battle for second place behind race leader Filipe Albuquerque.

As the GTP field accelerated down the front straight toward Turn 1, the two frontrunners leaned into each other fighting for position. The heavy side-to-side contact sent both top-tier prototypes sliding at high speed into the outer walls, instantly destroying both cars and ending the race under a full-course caution.

Following a comprehensive post-race review, IMSA penalised the #6 Porsche Penske Motorsport entry with a post-race time penalty equivalent to a five-minute stop-and-hold for incident responsibility under Article 57.3.5. Estre was individually assigned a two-race probation for unjustifiable risk under Articles 30.2.4 and 57.3.3.

title: Bold prediction for Broncos’ Bo Nix entering 2026 NFL season
description: Can Broncos quarterback Bo Nix really do this?
fullText:
The NFL MVP conversation usually starts with the same names: Patrick Mahomes. Josh Allen. Lamar Jackson. Drake Maye.

It's time to add in Bo Nix. Nix threw for 3,931 yards and 25 touchdowns last season while adding another 356 yards and five scores on the ground. More importantly, Denver went 14-3, earned the AFC's No. 1 seed, and reached the AFC Championship Game after Nix suffered a broken ankle in the Divisional Round.

MORE: 5 most improved NFL offenses entering 2026-2027 season

Now he gets Jaylen Waddle, a healthy ankle, and another year with Sean Payton. And the early returns are interesting.

Jan 17, 2026; Denver, CO, USA; Denver Broncos quarterback Bo Nix (10) reacts after winning an AFC Divisional Round playoff game against the Buffalo Bills at Empower Field at Mile High. Mandatory Credit: Ron Chenoy-Imagn Images

Denver Post reporter Luca Evans offered this observation after watching Nix early in camp: "Bo Nix looks considerably better + more poised + accurate" than at the same point last year.

That is the sentence that has my attention.

MORE: Predicting the AFC playoff teams ahead of the 2026-2027 NFL season

This isn't Nix trying to prove he belongs anymore. He already proved he can win. The next jump has to come in efficiency, accuracy, and command – exactly the areas Evans is already noticing.

Then Denver added Waddle, giving Nix an explosive weapon he openly said brings something the offense had been missing. Davis Webb taking over play-calling also gives Nix an offensive coordinator who spent the previous three seasons working directly with him as quarterbacks coach.

Jan 4, 2026; Denver, Colorado, USA; Denver Broncos quarterback Bo Nix (10) runs with the ball against the Los Angeles Chargers during the first half at Empower Field at Mile High. Mandatory Credit: Isaiah J. Downing-Imagn Images Credit: IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect (Reuters)

An MVP prediction requires team success, too. Denver already checked that box last year. If Nix turns 25 passing touchdowns into 30-plus, pushes beyond 4,000 yards and Denver again wins 12 or 13 games, the conversation changes quickly.

Nix himself said this offseason that winning an MVP is one of his goals. I'm starting to think that sounds less crazy than it did in June.

title: Saquon Barkley dislikes joint practices, but they aren't going away
description: Being a contact sport, it is always good to hit someone other than your own team on the football field
fullText:
Philadelphia Eagles running back Saquon Barkley is not a fan of joint practices beyond one day.

Most NFL teams will have two or three days of joint practices throughout the preseason to break the monotony. Some players are fans of them, and some are not. Saquon Barkley is the latter. Joint practices are held so teams can see how players go up against opponents they don't see every day in practice.

Being a contact sport, it is always good to hit someone other than your own team on the football field. But emotions are already high in your own camp. When it comes to ramping up competition to earn a spot in the summer heat, sometimes emotions spill over into throwing hands, grabbing facemasks, jawing with the other team, etc.

The Eagles would hold joint practice with the New England Patriots, and Eagles tackle Lane Johnson and Patriots linebacker K.J. Britt would get into an altercation, prompting Barkley's response when asked about the benefits of a joint practice afterward.

"I'm the wrong guy to ask because I hate joint practices, to be honest. I think one day is good," Barkley said.

"More times than not nothing good comes out of it. When you have the work it's good, but then you get the pushing, the shoving and someone says this about you and it's 'I don't know about that but you're this.' It's immature when you get to that level. I have to do a better job, too, because I'm a little troublemaker sometimes, but I was good this week."

Even though Barkley is not a fan, it doesn't appear that the NFL will move away from joint practices any time soon, especially since coaches and coordinators seem more on board with the idea than the players. It gives coaches a chance to scheme up things against different looks that they do not get every day in practice from scout teams within their own organizations.

title: Caitlin Clark’s surprise defensive highlight sends Fever fans into frenzy
description: Caitlin Clark struggled offensively against Dallas, but a slow-motion replay of her perfectly timed block quickly captured fans’ attention.
fullText:
Caitlin Clark's surprise defensive highlight sends Fever fans into frenzy originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

Caitlin Clark endured one of her most difficult offensive performances of the season Thursday, but the Indiana Fever star still found a way to produce one of the night's most memorable highlights. Clark finished with 10 points on 4-of-15 shooting as the Fever suffered a 91-85 road loss to the Dallas Wings. The defeat snapped Indiana's five-game winning streak and dropped the team to 24-13.

The two-time All-Star was unable to find a consistent scoring rhythm, but she contributed four rebounds, nine assists, one steal and one block. That lone rejection quickly attracted attention after the Fever shared a slow-motion replay of it.

"Caitlin Clark sends it back," Indiana wrote on Instagram.

The play unfolded midway through the second quarter when Arike Ogunbowale found Maddy Siegrist moving toward the basket. Siegrist appeared to have a favorable matchup. The Wings forward stands 6-foot-2, while Clark is a 6-foot guard who is known far more for her scoring and passing than her shot-blocking ability.

Clark refused to surrender an easy basket.

Siegrist gathered the ball and elevated for a layup, but Clark stayed with the play and perfectly timed her jump. She met the attempt near its release point and knocked the ball out of bounds.

The slow-motion replay showed Clark tracking the ball throughout the sequence and avoiding contact with Siegrist's arm. Her execution transformed what initially looked like a routine scoring opportunity into a clean defensive stop.

Fans responding to the clip celebrated the unexpected highlight. One joked that Clark had summoned the "SWAT TEAM," while others described the block as tough or said the Wings would not score on her watch.

MORE: Angel Reese breaks her own WNBA record during Dream's West Coast trip

Clark's shot never arrived Thursday, but her overall production demonstrated why Indiana can still lean on her when she is not scoring efficiently. Her nine assists helped create offense for a Fever team that received 37 points from Kelsey Mitchell and 14 from Aliyah Boston. Clark also reached 1,700 career points during the contest, becoming the fastest player in WNBA history to record at least 1,700 points, 400 rebounds and 700 assists.

None of it was enough to prevent Dallas from ending Indiana's winning streak. The Wings received a season-high scoring performance from Ogunbowale and repeatedly answered the Fever's attempts to rally. Clark and Indiana will have a chance to respond Saturday against the New York Liberty at Barclays Center. Tipoff is scheduled for 7 p.m. ET.

The Fever star would prefer to make headlines with her shooting in New York. Against Dallas, however, it was an emphatic defensive play that left fans talking.

title: 3 Packers who need to bounce back in Week 2 preseason game vs. Broncos
description: Who needs to bounce back for the Packers in preseason Week 2? Here are three players.
fullText:
The Green Bay Packers return to the field Friday night to face the Denver Broncos after losing the preseason opener 28-9 to the Pittsburgh Steelers. For some players, it will be a chance to build on a strong performance while others need to forget about last week and take advantage of a new opportunity to impress the coaching staff.

Here are three Packers who need to bounce back in Week 2 of the preseason:

Fighting to keep his spot in the starting lineup, Nixon didn't do himself many favors against the Steelers. His missed tackle after a completion to rookie wide receiver Germie Benard led to a 25-yard pickup, an uncharacteristic mistake coming off a season in which he missed only four in 17 games.

Nixon didn't exactly help himself in practice this week, giving up a big gain to receiver Savion Williams while playing on the third-team defense on Wednesday. Matt LaFleur laughed off Nixon's "punished" comment, but last week the veteran cornerback played like someone who isn't competing for his job. A bounce-back game against the Broncos that shows he's not backing down from the competition would be a step in the right direction.

Belton was Green Bay's lowest-rated offensive lineman by Pro Football Focus in the Steelers game, struggling particularly as a run blocker.

At the beginning of the offseason, he was penciled in as the starting right guard. Since then, rookie Jager Burton has continued to get more reps with the 1s while Belton is primarily spending time at both tackle spots behind starters Jordan Morgan and Zach Bako-Bewele.

A second-round pick a year ago, Belton was expected to be a serious contender for a starting role. Right now, it appears he's on the outside looking in.

Nixon wasn't the only corner who struggled in Pittsburgh. Simpson slipped on a 74-yard slant to rookie wide receiver Kaden Wetjen to set up the Steelers' second touchdown, gave up a five-yard touchdown to Wetjen, and then committed a 24-yard pass interference penalty.

Simpson didn't make the Packers' initial roster last year but was brought back to the practice squad and then signed to the active roster before the end of the season. Last week, 26 of his 49 defensive snaps came in the slot, and the team is still searching for the best option to be Javon Bullard's backup. Simpson could give himself a better shot at making the roster if he shows he's a viable option in these last two preseason games.
